title: Iroquois Beaver Wars
summary: In the 1600s the Haudenosaunee (Six Nations) fought wars across the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley, and later used them to claim rights over Kentucky.
bodyMarkdown:
In the 1600s the Haudenosaunee, a confederacy the English called the Iroquois, fought a long series of wars against neighboring peoples. They were then the Five Nations: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca. The Tuscarora joined in the early 1700s, making them the Six Nations. Historians call these conflicts the [Beaver Wars](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beaver_Wars), and date them from about 1640 to the Great Peace of Montreal in 1701.

The fighting was tied to the fur trade. Beaver had grown scarce in the Haudenosaunee homeland in what is now New York. With firearms traded from the Dutch, Iroquois warriors pressed west and north to control the trade routes and hunting grounds. They broke the Huron confederacy around 1648 to 1650 and turned on the [Erie](/stories/erie-the-cat-nation/) and Neutral nations in the 1650s. Wars with the [Susquehannock](/stories/susquehannock-and-the-ohio-valley-door/) and peoples farther west carried the fighting across the Great Lakes and into the Ohio Valley.

Disease shaped these wars as much as guns did. Smallpox struck Iroquois towns in the 1630s, and many raids were "mourning wars," fought to take captives who could be adopted to replace the dead. Epidemics also spread along trade routes into the interior and reduced populations there.

What happened to the peoples who lived in or near Kentucky in this period is hard to pin down. Early written references to groups in the Bluegrass and the middle Ohio Valley are mostly secondhand reports, and some groups had already moved or merged with others before Europeans recorded them. Stories such as the [Mosopelea and Ofo](/stories/mosopelea-ofo-the-ohio-valley/) trace some of those movements. The land was not empty, but who lived where, and when, is often uncertain.

By the 1700s the Iroquois wanted to control the Ohio Valley, and they claimed rights over it as conquerors. The [Shawnee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee), who lived and hunted in Kentucky, disputed that claim. Shawnee towns such as [Lower Shawneetown](/stories/lower-shawneetown-greenup-county/) on the Ohio were part of that use of the land.

The rival claims came to a head in 1768. At the [Treaty of Fort Stanwix](https://grokipedia.com/page/Treaty_of_Fort_Stanwix_%281768%29), Six Nations leaders meeting with [Sir William Johnson](/people/#william-johnson) sold their claim to Kentucky land east of the Tennessee River, most of the present state, to the British Crown. The Shawnee, who used much of that land, did not agree to the sale, and the deal helped set up the frontier wars that followed. The full story of the treaty is told in [Treaty of Fort Stanwix, 1768](/stories/treaty-of-fort-stanwix-1768/).
Source: [Henderson, Dispelling the Myth: 17th- and 18th-Century Indian Life in Kentucky (Register of the KHS, 1992)](https://preservationkentucky.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Dispelling-the-Myth-17th-18th-Century-Indian-Life-in-KY.pdf)
